match.reason: Neither bank point teaches antigenic drift or shift: the gene flow and genetic drift point covers population allele frequencies, and the vaccination point covers how vaccines train the immune system, which is related but not the same idea.

draft.title: Antigenic drift and shift
card: Antigens are molecules on a virus that the immune system recognises. Memory cells made after an infection or vaccine only match antigens they have met before.
small changes in viral antigens, caused by point mutations as the virus copies its genetic material. Over time, these build up and the antigens no longer match what the immune system remembers.
a sudden, large change in viral antigens. It happens when two different influenza viruses infect the same cell and swap whole segments of genetic material, producing a new antigen combination.
Both changes make older immunity less effective. This is why the influenza vaccine is updated regularly to match the viruses that are circulating.
draft.remember: Drift is small, gradual change from mutation. Shift is sudden, large change from swapped genetic material.

a.q: Which description fits antigenic drift in an influenza virus?
opts: Point mutations slowly change the viral antigens
Two viruses swap segments to make a new antigen set
The host's memory cells change the viral antigens
Vaccination changes the antigens on the virus
a.why: Drift is a gradual build-up of small changes from point mutations. Swapping segments between two viruses describes shift, which is sudden and large. Memory cells and vaccines do not change the virus's antigens.
a.clue: Think small changes that build up over time.

b.q: A flu season in Geelong is caused by a virus with a very different antigen set. It formed when two flu viruses infected one cell and swapped segments. Why does most of the population have little protection?
opts: Memory cells do not match the new antigens
Memory cells were destroyed by the earlier viruses
The new virus does not trigger any immune response
Point mutations in the host cells removed memory
b.why: A sudden big change in antigens is antigenic shift. Memory cells only match antigens they have met, so they do not recognise the new set. The virus can still trigger a new response, but it takes time to build.
b.clue: Memory cells only recognise antigens they have met before.

a.best: Point mutations slowly change the viral antigens

b.best: Memory cells do not match the new antigens
